topic: The Doctor Who Was Locked Away for Being Right
strongest_angle: In 1847, obstetrician Ignaz Semmelweis proved — with real hospital mortality data — that doctors were killing new mothers by not washing their hands between autopsies and deliveries. He cut deaths from roughly 18% to about 2% in a single year with chlorinated lime handwashing. The medical establishment rejected the finding because it implied gentlemen doctors were the vector, not the cure. Semmelweis was pushed out, his ideas ridiculed, and he died in an asylum at 47 — beaten by guards, days after being committed — 20 years before germ theory proved he was right the entire time.
hook_candidates: In 1847 a doctor proved handwashing saves lives. His colleagues had him locked in an asylum instead of washing their hands.
He cut the death rate by 90% with soap and chlorinated lime. The medical establishment called him insane for it.
The doctor who discovered germ theory 20 years early died forgotten in an asylum — beaten by the guards who put him there.

key_facts.fact: At Vienna General Hospital's maternity division, patients were split between two clinics: the First Clinic, staffed by doctors and medical students who also performed autopsies, and the Second Clinic, staffed by midwives who did not. From 1840–1846, maternal mortality averaged roughly 98.4 deaths per 1,000 births in the First Clinic versus about 36.2 per 1,000 in the Second — nearly triple the death rate in the doctors' ward.
key_facts.source: James Lind Library, 'Ignaz Phillip Semmelweis' studies of death in childbirth', jameslindlibrary.org

key_facts.fact: In April 1847, mortality in Semmelweis's First Clinic had reached 18.3%. In May 1847 he ordered doctors and medical students to disinfect their hands with a chlorinated lime solution before examining women in labor. By June the death rate fell to 2.2%, and stayed similarly low through July and August.
key_facts.source: James Lind Library / risk-engineering.org, 'Semmelweis and puerperal fever'

key_facts.fact: Semmelweis correctly identified the cause as 'cadaverous particles' carried on the hands of doctors coming directly from autopsies to deliveries — decades before Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch established germ theory. Colleagues rejected the explanation; the dominant theory of the time held disease was caused by 'miasma' (bad air), and many physicians were personally offended by the implication that their own hands were the vector — one contemporary is recorded as insisting 'a gentleman's hands are clean.'
key_facts.source: Reader's Digest / MedBound Hub summaries of Semmelweis historiography

key_facts.fact: Ostracized by the Vienna medical establishment, Semmelweis eventually left for Budapest, grew increasingly erratic under the strain of professional rejection, and in 1865 was committed to the Landesirrenanstalt asylum in Vienna. He died there weeks later, at age 47, reportedly after being beaten by asylum guards — the same year Joseph Lister began publishing on antiseptic surgery using the germ theory Semmelweis had no formal framework to prove.
key_facts.source: Science History Institute biography; NCBI/PMC historiographical review of Semmelweis (PMC12720402)

key_facts.fact: Semmelweis's handwashing protocol was only widely vindicated after his death, once Pasteur's and Koch's germ theory of disease (1860s–1880s) gave doctors a causal mechanism to accept what his mortality data had already shown two decades earlier.
key_facts.source: Science History Institute; Wellcome Collection, 'The father of handwashing'

practitioner_notes: Semmelweis is a well-documented, frequently-cited case in medical history and patient-safety education (the 'Semmelweis reflex' is a named concept for rejecting evidence that contradicts existing norms), which makes it easy to source rigorously while still landing as a dramatic, character-driven story for the channel's 'hidden figures' pillar. Multiple independent sources agree on the core mortality figures (~18% to ~2%) though exact decimal points vary slightly by source (18.3%→2.2% vs. 18%→~1-2%) — script should use a rounded, defensible figure and avoid over-precision.
open_questions: Primary sources disagree on decimal precision for the mortality drop (18.3%→2.2% vs. rounder figures elsewhere) — use the more specific, sourced figures (James Lind Library / risk-engineering.org) and round for narration.

The 'beaten by guards' detail is reported by multiple secondary sources but should be framed as 'reportedly' since asylum records from 1865 are not fully verifiable first-hand from this research pass.
